title: Sudden severe headache
blurb: Adult with a headache that reached maximum intensity within a minute, six hours ago.
curriculum_note: Neurologic complaint and case are ILG 10 and ILG 11 on the PCM I schedule. Original case; not a prediction of any exam station. This case is deliberately time-critical: the plan should reflect a disposition rather than a routine follow-up interval.

doorway: Presents to the family medicine clinic with a headache.
Vital signs are supplied at this station.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, and discuss your plan with the patient.

patient.name: Ellis Tran
patient.persona: A graphic designer with a long history of migraines who is certain this one is different. Squinting against the light, speaking quietly. Came in because her husband insisted. Frightened but trying to be reasonable about it.
patient.affect: Photophobic and uncomfortable; keeps her eyes half-closed. Increasingly anxious as the encounter goes on.
patient.opening: I got this headache about six hours ago and it came on like someone hit me. I get migraines, but this is not my migraine.
empathy_replies: I appreciate that. I keep telling myself I'm overreacting.

cc: Sudden severe headache for 6 hours

HPI: 28 yo f with an 11-year history of migraines presents to clinic c/o a headache that began 6 hours ago while lifting a box and reached maximum intensity in under one minute. Pain is occipital, radiating into the neck, 10/10, constant and unrelenting since onset. She describes it as the worst headache of her life and explicitly unlike her usual migraine, which builds over hours, is unilateral and responds to sumatriptan. Sumatriptan taken 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg gave no relief. Worse with light, bending forward and coughing. Associated with neck stiffness, two episodes of vomiting without preceding nausea, and a transient greying of vision at onset without a fall. Denies focal weakness, numbness, speech change, visual change, seizure, fever, chills, rash, sick contacts and head trauma. Concerned this is a ruptured aneurysm; her mother had one at 49.

PMH: Migraines since age 17. No hypertension.
PSH: None. No hospitalizations.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN; ibuprofen 800 mg PRN; oral contraceptive 1 tab daily.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with husband. Current smoker, 0.5 ppd x8 years. Wine a few times weekly. Denies illicit drug use including cocaine and stimulants. LMP 2 weeks ago, no chance of pregnancy.
FH: Mother with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49, survived. Father 61, well. One brother, healthy.
Allergies: NKDA.
ROS: Neurologic - admits headache, photophobia, transient near-syncope; denies weakness, numbness, seizure, speech change. HEENT - admits neck stiffness and photophobia; denies visual change and diplopia. General - admits vomiting; denies fever, chills, night sweats and weight loss.

Vitals: T 98.8 F oral, P 92 bpm, BP 162/95 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5'6", Wt 141 lbs

General: Young woman lying still with eyes closed, shielding them from the light, in moderate distress from pain. Alert, oriented and answering appropriately.
HEENT: PERLA. Fundoscopy limited by photophobia; no papilledema seen in the portion visualised. Corneal reflex refused.
Neck: Marked resistance and pain on passive flexion. Rotation comfortable. Kernig and Brudzinski negative.
Heart: RRR, S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.
Lungs: CTA bilaterally anterior and posterior.
Neuro: CN II-XII intact as tested - visual fields full, EOM intact, facial sensation and strength symmetric, palate elevates symmetrically, tongue midline. Strength 5/5 in all four extremities, no pronator drift. Sensation to light touch and pinprick intact and symmetric. DTRs 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, patellae and Achilles; plantars downgoing. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact, Romberg negative. Gait steady though guarded.
Skin: No rash, petechiae or purpura.
Osteopathic: Marked suboccipital and cervical paraspinal hypertonicity with tenderness, C1-C4; T1-T4 paraspinal tissue texture change. Cervical motion guarded.
P: 1. Transfer immediately to the emergency department by EMS for urgent noncontrast head CT and specialist assessment. Additional testing after a negative head CT depends on time from onset, imaging quality and residual suspicion; discuss lumbar puncture and/or vascular imaging through the emergency team rather than treating every negative CT identically. Obtain CBC, BMP and coagulation testing as appropriate; provide clinician-directed symptom control. Explain that a thunderclap headache cannot wait and the patient must not drive; emergency department disposition now.

2. Lumbar puncture with cell count, glucose, protein and culture as above; do not delay empiric antibiotics if fever or clinical deterioration develops; educate the patient and her husband on the warning signs of deterioration.

3. MRI of the brain with contrast once the emergency evaluation is complete; discontinue the combined oral contraceptive; refer to neurology; educate on smoking cessation, which compounds the same vascular risk.
OMT deferred: no cervical manipulation until an intracranial bleed is excluded.

ideal_encounter_extras: Ask how fast the headache reached its peak, not just when it started. 'Sudden' and 'maximal within a minute' are different claims, and only the second one is a thunderclap.

Ask how this headache differs from her usual migraine. A fifteen-year migraine history is the reason a clinician might dismiss this, and her own answer is the strongest argument against dismissing it.

P: 1. Transfer immediately to the emergency department by EMS for urgent noncontrast head CT and specialist assessment. Additional testing after a negative head CT depends on time from onset, imaging quality and residual suspicion; discuss lumbar puncture and/or vascular imaging through the emergency team rather than treating every negative CT identically. Obtain CBC, BMP and coagulation testing as appropriate; provide clinician-directed symptom control. Explain that a thunderclap headache cannot wait and the patient must not drive; emergency department disposition now. Use plain language, pause between steps, and invite teach-back.

2. Lumbar puncture with cell count, glucose, protein and culture as above; do not delay empiric antibiotics if fever or clinical deterioration develops; educate the patient and her husband on the warning signs of deterioration.

3. MRI of the brain with contrast once the emergency evaluation is complete; discontinue the combined oral contraceptive; refer to neurology; educate on smoking cessation, which compounds the same vascular risk.

history.text: About six hours ago, mid-morning.
It went from nothing to unbearable in less than a minute. Like being hit in the back of the head. It's the worst headache I've ever had.
The back of my head, and it goes down into my neck.
Ten out of ten. I've had migraines since I was seventeen and they never got close to this.
It hasn't let up once. It's been constant for six hours.
I was picking up a box of files at my desk. I didn't hit my head or fall or anything.
I took my sumatriptan two hours ago and 800 of ibuprofen. Nothing. Normally the sumatriptan works within an hour.
Light makes it worse — that's why I'm squinting. And it gets worse when I bend forward or cough.
I've had migraines since I was seventeen. They build up over hours, they're on one side, and they respond to the sumatriptan. This is nothing like that.
My neck feels stiff. It hurts to put my chin down.
I threw up twice on the way here. It came out of nowhere, I wasn't even nauseated first.
Right when it hit, everything went grey for a few seconds. I grabbed the desk. I don't think I actually passed out.
No weakness, nothing numb, my speech is fine. My vision's normal apart from the light hurting. No seizures.
No fever, no chills. No rash. No night sweats, and my weight is the same. Nobody around me has been sick.
Just the migraines. My blood pressure's always been fine. Nothing else.
I've never had surgery and I've never been admitted anywhere.
Sumatriptan when I get a migraine, ibuprofen as needed, and a birth control pill every day.
None that I know of.
About half a pack a day. Eight years or so.
A glass of wine a few nights a week.
No. Nothing like that, ever.
I am a graphic designer and work from home.
My last period was 2 weeks ago.
My mother had a brain aneurysm that burst when she was forty-nine. She survived it. My father's sixty-one and healthy, and I have one brother who's fine.
I know my migraines and this isn't one. My mother's aneurysm — that's what I keep thinking about.
I am worried about getting to follow-up and knowing whom to call if I get worse.
I live with my husband.
I do not think there is a chance I am pregnant.
I got this headache about six hours ago and it came on like someone hit me. I get migraines, but this is not my migraine.

model_note.S:
cc: Sudden severe headache for 6 hours

HPI: 28 yo f with an 11-year history of migraines presents to clinic c/o a headache that began 6 hours ago while lifting a box and reached maximum intensity in under one minute. Pain is occipital, radiating into the neck, 10/10, constant and unrelenting since onset. She describes it as the worst headache of her life and explicitly unlike her usual migraine, which builds over hours, is unilateral and responds to sumatriptan. Sumatriptan taken 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg gave no relief. Worse with light, bending forward and coughing. Associated with neck stiffness, two episodes of vomiting without preceding nausea, and a transient greying of vision at onset without a fall. Denies focal weakness, numbness, speech change, visual change, seizure, fever, chills, rash, sick contacts and head trauma. Concerned this is a ruptured aneurysm; her mother had one at 49.

PMH: Migraines since age 17. No hypertension.
PSH: None. No hospitalizations.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN; ibuprofen 800 mg PRN; oral contraceptive 1 tab daily.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with husband. Current smoker, 0.5 ppd x8 years. Wine a few times weekly. Denies illicit drug use including cocaine and stimulants. LMP 2 weeks ago, no chance of pregnancy.
FH: Mother with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49, survived. Father 61, well. One brother, healthy.
Allergies: NKDA.
ROS: Neurologic - admits headache, photophobia, transient near-syncope; denies weakness, numbness, seizure, speech change. HEENT - admits neck stiffness and photophobia; denies visual change and diplopia. General - admits vomiting; denies fever, chills, night sweats and weight loss.

Patient concern: I am worried about getting to follow-up and knowing whom to call if I get worse.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.8 F oral, P 92 bpm, BP 162/95 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5'6", Wt 141 lbs

General: Young woman lying still with eyes closed, shielding them from the light, in moderate distress from pain. Alert, oriented and answering appropriately.
HEENT: PERLA. Fundoscopy limited by photophobia; no papilledema seen in the portion visualised. Corneal reflex refused.
Neck: Marked resistance and pain on passive flexion. Rotation comfortable. Kernig and Brudzinski negative.
Heart: RRR, S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, rubs or gallops.
Lungs: CTA bilaterally anterior and posterior.
Neuro: CN II-XII intact as tested - visual fields full, EOM intact, facial sensation and strength symmetric, palate elevates symmetrically, tongue midline. Strength 5/5 in all four extremities, no pronator drift. Sensation to light touch and pinprick intact and symmetric. DTRs 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, patellae and Achilles; plantars downgoing. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact, Romberg negative. Gait steady though guarded.
Skin: No rash, petechiae or purpura.
Osteopathic: Marked suboccipital and cervical paraspinal hypertonicity with tenderness, C1-C4; T1-T4 paraspinal tissue texture change. Cervical motion guarded.
P: 1. Transfer immediately to the emergency department by EMS for urgent noncontrast head CT and specialist assessment. Additional testing after a negative head CT depends on time from onset, imaging quality and residual suspicion; discuss lumbar puncture and/or vascular imaging through the emergency team rather than treating every negative CT identically. Obtain CBC, BMP and coagulation testing as appropriate; provide clinician-directed symptom control. Explain that a thunderclap headache cannot wait and the patient must not drive; emergency department disposition now. Agree on a practical contact and transportation plan; verify the patient can describe the urgent warning signs.

2. Lumbar puncture with cell count, glucose, protein and culture as above; do not delay empiric antibiotics if fever or clinical deterioration develops; educate the patient and her husband on the warning signs of deterioration.

3. MRI of the brain with contrast once the emergency evaluation is complete; discontinue the combined oral contraceptive; refer to neurology; educate on smoking cessation, which compounds the same vascular risk.
OMT deferred: no cervical manipulation until an intracranial bleed is excluded.
